notes.meaning: Peter speaks to the church leaders, who are called elders. He was an apostle and could have given orders, but he calls himself a "fellow elder," one of them. He does not claim to rule over all pastors and churches. He had seen Jesus suffer, and he shares the hope of the glory that will be shown when Christ returns.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching sees "fellow elder" as Peter showing the same humility he asks of others, as Paul sometimes did. In this view it does not cancel Peter's place as first among the apostles.

notes.meaning: Elders are to care for God's people the way a shepherd cares for sheep. That means feeding them with God's Word, guiding them and watching over them. Peter was probably remembering Jesus telling him, "Feed my sheep." They should serve gladly, not because they are forced and not for money, and they must not boss people around, because the flock belongs to God and they should lead by their own good example.

Jesus is the Chief Shepherd. He is over all the other shepherds, and they answer to him. When he comes again, faithful leaders will receive a "crown of glory." It is like the victory wreath given to winners in the ancient games, but this one will never wither, and it is far better than any money or power.

Younger people should respect the older leaders and listen to them. But everyone, young and old, is to put on humility like clothing. Peter's word pictures a servant tying on a work apron, and he may be remembering Jesus washing the disciples' feet. He quotes Proverbs: God stands against the proud but gives grace, his kind and undeserved help, to the humble.

Since God helps the humble, bow low before his strong hand, even in hard times. Don't push yourself forward. God will lift you up at the right time. That is his wise time, not the time we pick, whether in this life or in heaven.

Throw all your worries onto God, like tossing a heavy load off your back. Peter is echoing Psalm 55:22. Every kind of worry can go to him: about yourself, your family, today or tomorrow. You can do this because he truly cares about you.

While you trust God, stay clear-headed and awake. The devil is your enemy, like an opponent in a court case. He is pictured as a hungry, roaring lion looking for someone to destroy. For these readers, his roar was mainly persecution, meant to scare them into giving up their faith.

Don't run from the devil. Stand against him. Your strength is a firm faith in God. And you are not alone, because Christians all over the world face the same kinds of suffering, so God has not singled you out or turned against you.

Peter turns to hope. God is the source of every kind of grace, and he has called you through Christ to share his glory forever. Your suffering lasts only a short while compared with that. Then God himself will mend you, steady you, strengthen you and settle you, like a house set on a firm foundation.

differ.view: "Perfect" means God completing his work of grace in us, so that no weakness or defect remains.
"Perfect" means growing in holiness little by little. Even the best believers are not fully perfect in this life.

notes.meaning: Peter bursts into praise. All power belongs to God, and only to him, forever. If God rules over everything, his people have nothing to fear. "Amen" means "so be it."

Silvanus is the Silas who traveled with Paul. Peter calls him a faithful brother, and Silvanus likely carried the letter to the churches. Peter sums up his short letter. He wrote to encourage them and to promise them that this message of God's grace, his free gift of salvation, is true, so they should stand firm in it.

Peter sends greetings from the church where he is, a place he calls "Babylon." Those believers were chosen by God, just like the readers. Mark, probably the writer of the Gospel, also sends greetings. Peter calls him "my son" because Peter probably led him to faith.

differ.view: "Babylon" means the real city of Babylon, where many Jews lived. Peter, as apostle to the Jews, would naturally go there.
"Babylon" is a code name for Rome. It fits the letter's picture of Christians as exiles far from home.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics see "Babylon" as Rome and take it as evidence that Peter was in Rome. This supports their teaching about the bishop of Rome.

notes.meaning: Peter asks them to greet each other with a kiss of love. This was a normal warm greeting in those days, a sign of real love among believers. He ends by wishing peace to everyone who belongs to Christ. True peace comes from Christ alone.
